messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 64
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Warehouse Worker
  trauma_type: Captivity
  pcl5: 60

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Time of Day: The same time of day the event occurred, Animal Phobia: Talks or photos about snakes, Nighttime/Dark: Night-time or waking up in the dark
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Sleep: Going to sleep or lying in the dark, Reassurance Seeking: I keep asking others to reassure me that I am okay, Body Monitoring: constantly check body for signs of danger or injury
  Threat: Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
  Negative Appraisals: Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore, Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Rajan is a 64-year-old South Asian man who has been married for nearly four decades and works the early morning shift at a large distribution warehouse on the outskirts of the city. He was referred for psychological assessment following a disclosure to his primary care physician, though he had been carrying what happened to him largely in silence for almost two years.

The event that precipitated his current difficulties occurred during a visit to relatives in a rural area. Rajan was detained overnight by a group of men in what he describes as a partially underground storage structure — dark, earthen-walled, and airless. He was held for approximately eighteen hours, restrained and unable to leave, uncertain whether he would be released or harmed. At some point during the night, he became aware of movement near his feet and realised, in the near-total darkness, that there were snakes in the space with him. He remained motionless for hours, convinced that any movement would provoke a bite. He was eventually released unharmed, but the experience of absolute helplessness — pinned between human threat and animal danger, in the dark, in the early hours before dawn — left a mark that has not faded.

In the months that followed, Rajan found that certain moments in his daily life had become unbearable. The pre-dawn hours of his warehouse shift — the same time of day he had been held — began to feel charged with a formless dread he could not explain to colleagues. Photographs of snakes in a safety pamphlet posted near the loading dock once sent him to the bathroom shaking. Night-time itself, and the simple act of waking in the dark in his own bedroom, had become triggers that pulled him back into the storage room with a vividness he found almost physically painful. These moments of intrusion began to organise his behaviour: he started avoiding sleep, lying awake rather than surrendering to darkness, and when he did sleep, he kept a lamp burning on his side of the bed. He had also begun to check his body obsessively — pressing fingers along his arms and legs each morning, searching for signs of injury or illness he could not rationally account for — and he sought reassurance from his wife and adult children with an urgency that had begun to strain those relationships. His wife, who initially responded with patience, had grown quietly exhausted by his nightly need for confirmation that he was safe.

What Rajan had not anticipated was that the strategies he adopted to manage his distress were themselves keeping him in contact with the very cues he feared. Lying awake in the dark prolonged his exposure to the nighttime environment that triggered the memories; the lamp he kept on created a ritual that marked every night as dangerous, and his body-checking in the early warehouse hours drew his attention precisely to the time-of-day cues he was trying to outlast. The avoidance had become a kind of maintenance.

He had come to believe, with a quiet but settled certainty, that he simply could not cope if the memories were allowed to surface fully — that thinking about what happened would undo him entirely. This conviction sat alongside a deeper fear: that bad things happened to him because he was powerless to prevent them, that the world had shown him something true about his own vulnerability. These appraisals fed directly into his vigilance. Certain that threat could arrive without warning, he had developed a habit of looking behind him on the warehouse floor, scanning the shadows between shelving units, remaining hyperalert throughout his shift in ways that left him exhausted by mid-morning. At night, the same sense of helplessness made it harder to feel safe — the darkness outside his bedroom window seemed less like ordinary night and more like the absence of protection.

There were moments, he admitted, when he was not sure his life was worth continuing. He said this quietly, without drama, as though reporting a weather condition.

What finally brought Rajan to seek help was a conversation with his youngest son, who had noticed that his father had not slept properly in months and who asked, gently, whether something was wrong. Rajan came to the first session hoping, more than anything, to be able to sleep in the dark again — and to stop feeling, at 64, like a man who had run out of safety.
